title: Temporal Memory and Minicolumns
intro: Hierarchical Temporal Memory (HTM) models how a layer of pyramidal neurons, arranged in minicolumns, learns sequences and predicts what comes next. Its central idea is that most of a neuron's synapses are not for firing it but for predicting when it will fire. Temporal memory (TM) is HTM's sequence memory: it takes the active minicolumns produced by the spatial pooler and chooses which cells inside them fire, so the same input is represented differently in different temporal contexts, and the layer can anticipate the next input even in high-order sequences.

blocks.text: A neuron with thousands of synapses

A typical cortical pyramidal neuron has several thousand excitatory synapses, yet classic point-neuron models, including the LIF neuron (#/brain/snn/neuron-models/lif), sum them all into one number. Hawkins and Ahmad (2016) argue that a pyramidal cell has three functionally distinct input zones:

items: Proximal dendrites, near the cell body: a few hundred synapses whose summed input can make the cell fire. These carry the feedforward input and define what the cell responds to, its classic receptive field.

Distal (basal) dendrites: most of the synapses, grouped into many independent segments. When roughly 10 to 20 nearby synapses on one segment are active together they trigger an NMDA spike, a local dendritic event that does not make the cell fire but depolarises it. HTM calls this the predictive state: the cell is primed to fire first if its feedforward input arrives.
Apical dendrites, reaching up to L1: receive top-down feedback and can also depolarise the cell, letting expectations from higher regions bias which cells win.

blocks.text: Because each distal segment recognises its own small pattern, one neuron can recognise dozens of different contexts in which it should expect to fire. That is a big step up in capacity from a point neuron.

blocks.alt: Two panels. The left panel draws a pyramidal neuron: a dark triangular cell body with short blue dendrites close to it labelled proximal, feedforward input; longer green branches below labelled basal distal, context from the same layer; a long trunk rising to a purple tuft at the top labelled apical tuft, in L1, feedback from higher areas; and a dashed axon leaving downwards. The right panel shows the HTM model of the same cell: a triangle labelled cell with a proximal zone below it fed by five feedforward input bits; three green basal segments and two purple apical segments to its left, each a row of six synapse dots, some filled to show active presynaptic cells; the lowest basal segment has five of six dots filled and is marked as firing; an arrow leaves the cell as output.
blocks.caption: The three input zones on a real pyramidal neuron (left) and in the HTM neuron model (right). Proximal input can make the cell fire; a basal or apical segment that detects its pattern only makes the cell predictive.

blocks.text: Minicolumns, bursting and context
In HTM a layer is a sheet of minicolumns. All cells in a minicolumn share the same feedforward input, so they all respond to the same feature. What distinguishes them is context. When input arrives:

items: If one or more cells in an activated minicolumn were in the predictive state, those cells fire first and fast inhibition silences their neighbours. Activity is very sparse and says not just 'B' but 'B in the context of A'.

If no cell was predicted, the input is a surprise and every cell in the minicolumn fires. This is called bursting. Bursting means 'B, in no context I recognise', and it turns on predictions for every way B has continued before.

Learning: in a bursting minicolumn one cell, the winner, is chosen (the one with the best partially matching segment, or the least used) and grows a new distal segment with synapses onto cells that were active a moment ago. Next time the same context occurs that cell will be predicted.

blocks.text: So the same input B is represented by different cells after A than after X. That is what lets a temporal memory learn high-order sequences: after A B C it can predict D, while after X B C it predicts Y, even though both share B C. A first-order model, which only looks at the current input, could never tell these apart.

blocks.alt: Two panels, each showing six minicolumns drawn as tall rounded boxes holding four cells. In both, the same three minicolumns are highlighted in yellow as driven by the input C. In the left panel, labelled not predicted, all four cells in each highlighted minicolumn are filled red, twelve bursting cells in all. In the right panel, labelled predicted, only one cell in each highlighted minicolumn is filled blue, each with a dashed ring showing it was predictive, three cells in all.
blocks.caption: Bursting versus prediction. An unexpected input fires every cell in its minicolumns; an expected one fires only the cells the context had primed, so the same input gets a different, sparse code in each context.

blocks.text: The plot runs a simplified temporal memory: 64 minicolumns, each input symbol activating a fixed set of 6 of them. The first curve is the share of active minicolumns that burst (unpredicted), the second the share that were correctly predicted. On the first pass through the sequence everything bursts, because nothing has been learned. From the second pass on the network predicts almost every step, and bursting drops to zero even for the two sequences that share the middle B C, because the cells for B after A differ from the cells for B after X. Try two cells per minicolumn and a high threshold: capacity for distinct contexts shrinks. Real HTM adds permanence values, gradual reinforcement and forgetting, which this sim leaves out.
Sparse distributed representations

HTM codes everything as sparse distributed representations (SDRs): large binary vectors, typically about 2 percent active. With, say, 2048 cells and 40 active, random SDRs almost never overlap by chance, so a segment that matches 15 of the 40 can detect a pattern reliably even with noise or missing bits. A cell can also match a union of several SDRs at once without much confusion, which is how a bursting minicolumn can hold several predictions. These properties are why HTM uses sparse binary codes, and they map naturally onto spiking networks, where at any moment most neurons are silent.
The spatial pooler

Before temporal memory, HTM's spatial pooler turns arbitrary input into SDRs with a fixed sparsity. Each minicolumn connects to a random subset of input bits, the most strongly driven minicolumns win via local inhibition (a k-winners-take-all), and the winners' connections are strengthened by a Hebbian rule. Boosting raises the excitability of rarely used minicolumns so all of them get used, a form of homeostasis (compare the BCM rule at #/brain/snn/learning-rules/stdp-bcm).
States and data structures

items: Per cell: lists of distal segments; per segment: a list of synapses (presynaptic cell index, permanence).

At each step t: activeColumns (from the SP), activeCells, winnerCells (one learning cell per active column), activeSegments (connected-synapse overlap with activeCells ≥ activationThreshold), matchingSegments (potential-synapse overlap ≥ minThreshold), and the predictive cells implied by activeSegments.

Typical NuPIC defaults (hedged; check your release): 2048 columns, 32 cells per column, activationThreshold 13, minThreshold 10, maxNewSynapseCount 20, initialPermanence 0.21, connectedPermanence 0.5, permanenceIncrement 0.1, permanenceDecrement 0.1, predictedSegmentDecrement 0 (or a small value such as 0.001–0.01 when punishment is used), up to 255 segments per cell and 255 synapses per segment.

blocks.text: The algorithm

This follows the temporal memory pseudocode in Numenta's BAMI book and the description in Cui, Ahmad & Hawkins (2016), simplified for readability. Everything at step t uses the previous step's active cells, winner cells and segment states.
Learning, line by line

items: Reinforce: on a segment that correctly predicted (or best matched) the current input, synapses to previously active cells are incremented and all other synapses on the segment are decremented. This is Hebbian (pre before post) learning with a built-in depression term, structurally similar to pair-based STDP with a causal window of one time step.

Grow: new synapses are added from the segment to a random sample of previous winner cells, up to maxNewSynapseCount active synapses per segment. Sampling winner cells rather than all active cells is what makes the representation context-specific: during a burst, all cells are active but only one per column is a winner.
Create segment: if no segment matches at all, the least-used cell in the bursting column gets a new segment. This is how a new context is allocated.

Punish: segments that predicted a column that did not become active are weakened by predictedSegmentDecrement. Many configurations set this to zero or very small, because aggressive punishment destroys legitimate alternative predictions in branching sequences.

New synapses start at initialPermanence. If it is below connectedPermanence (as in the NuPIC default 0.21 vs 0.5), a transition must be seen several times before it predicts, which filters noise; if it is just above (as in the simulator below, 0.51 vs 0.5), one exposure is enough — fast learning, but noise gets learned too.

blocks.text: Try it: learning A-B-C-D versus X-B-C-Y

The simulator below runs a small temporal memory: each symbol activates its own group of minicolumns (no spatial pooler), and cells, segments and permanences follow the algorithm above. The grid shows minicolumns × cells; the legend marks active, predictive, bursting and correctly predicted cells. The readout shows the current symbol, the symbols the layer currently predicts, and the anomaly score (the fraction of active columns that were not predicted).

widget.title: Temporal memory: learning A-B-C-D vs X-B-C-Y

items: Press Step a few times from a fresh start: every column bursts (all cells active) and the anomaly score is 1, because nothing has been learned yet.

Press Train ×10 once or twice, then Step through the sequences. Bursting turns into sparse activity (one cell per column), predicted cells are marked as correctly predicted, and the anomaly score falls towards 0. The first element of each sequence (A or X) may stay partly unpredicted, because which sequence comes next is not determined by what came before it.
Watch the step after C: following A-B-C the layer should predict only D; following X-B-C only Y. The context of A or X has been carried through B and C by which cells are active.

Reset, set Cells per minicolumn to 1 and train again. Now B and C have only one representation each, so after C the layer predicts both D and Y every time. Note that the anomaly score can still fall to zero, because it only counts active columns that were not predicted — extra wrong predictions are not penalised. The failure shows in the predicted-symbols readout: it never commits to one answer. This is the first-order limit.

Try 2 cells per minicolumn: two contexts per symbol is enough for this pair of sequences. Then raise the Segment activation threshold. Each symbol uses 4 minicolumns, so a segment can only connect to about 4 previous winner cells; with a threshold above that, segments never become active, nothing is predicted and every step bursts.
Use Play to watch learning unfold continuously, and change the Random seed to see that which cells end up representing each context is arbitrary, while the behaviour is not.

blocks.text: Capacity and high-order memory

With $N$ columns, $M$ cells per column and $w$ active columns, the same input can be represented in $M^w$ different contexts. For the Numenta defaults ($M = 32$, $w = 40$) that is $32^{40} = 2^{200}$, so running out of context codes is not the limit in practice (Hawkins & Ahmad 2016). The practical limits are the number of segments per cell and synapses per segment: each learned transition uses one segment on each of about w cells, so the number of transitions a layer can store scales with $N \times M \times$ (segments per cell). Hawkins & Ahmad (2016) and Cui, Ahmad & Hawkins (2016) show that such networks learn large numbers of high-order sequences and that performance degrades gracefully as segment limits are approached or cells are removed.

Because context is carried from step to step by which cells are active, temporal memory represents arbitrarily long context in principle; in practice, learning a dependency of length L requires seeing the sequence enough times for the context-specific cells to be allocated step by step along it. Long shared subsequences (A-B-C-…-Z versus X-B-C-…-Y) take longer to disambiguate, and the more often a shared subsequence is seen in different contexts, the more cells it consumes.
From HTM to spiking neurons

HTM is written with binary cells and discrete time steps, not spikes, but each piece has a spiking counterpart. The predictive state corresponds to a depolarised membrane, as in the dendrite of a two-compartment model (#/brain/snn/neuron-models/multicompartment). 'Predicted cells fire first and inhibit the rest' is a timing race that first-spike coding and fast inhibition implement naturally (#/brain/snn/encoding, and the winner-take-all sim on #/brain/neuroscience/cortical-columns). Growing synapses onto previously active cells is a causal, STDP-like rule (#/brain/snn/learning-rules/stdp-classical), with eligibility traces when the delay between steps is long. Whether real cortex implements temporal memory in exactly this way is not established; the dendritic NMDA spikes and their predictive depolarisation are.

Where this sits in the Thousand Brains Theory: the same machinery, with a location signal in place of the previous input as context, is proposed for L4 learning features at locations on an object (#/brain/neuroscience/cortical-columns/thousand-brains).
Spiking implementation notes

items: One HTM time step is one feedforward input window (tens of milliseconds). The distal plateau triggered by step t−1 activity must last into the window of step t; NMDA-like plateaus of 50–200 ms are in the right range for inputs presented every 20–100 ms.

Predicted cells must fire first and the minicolumn's inhibitory cells must silence the others within a few milliseconds; if not, every column bursts all the time. Build and test one minicolumn of excitatory cells plus a fast inhibitory interneuron before scaling up (see 'The HTM Neuron').

Winner selection during a burst needs a tie-breaker: in a spiking model, small random differences in excitability or a slightly stronger segment can make one cell fire first. Bouhadjar et al. (2022) build a spiking temporal-memory model in NEST along these lines and discuss the required parameter regime.

Segment growth is structural plasticity. On FPGAs or neuromorphic chips with fixed connectivity, pre-allocate a pool of potential synapses per segment with a permanence counter (e.g. 8-bit integer) and treat 'connected' as a threshold on the counter.

blocks.text: What to watch out for

items: Frequent bursting after long training usually means either the SP representation is drifting (see 'Spatial Pooler') or segments are being punished too hard.

Too-low activation thresholds create many spurious predictions; too-high thresholds mean nothing is ever predicted. A threshold of roughly half to three quarters of maxNewSynapseCount is a common starting point.
Unbounded segment growth on noisy streams wastes memory: cap segments per cell and synapses per segment, and remove the least-recently-used ones when full.
Repeating inputs (A-A-A-A) and sequences with no reset between them are handled differently by different implementations; some use an explicit 'reset' at sequence boundaries.
